title: The Panel Method: A Three-Frequency Dome, Framed on a Jig

chapters.title: Two ways to frame a dome
narration: On this hill stand two domes framed two different ways. One is the wedge dome: 120 members split from logs with a chainsaw, carrying their angles in their own shape. The other is a three-frequency dome of framed panels: 105 triangles, each one its own small frame of sawn sticks, built flat on a jig, skinned in the shop, and screwed to its neighbours on site. It is how most small timber domes built from bought plans are made, and it is worth knowing properly.

chapters.title: A popular build, tried and true
narration: The three-frequency five-eighths dome built from framed panels is one of the most popular small domes people build. It is tried and true: a great many of them are standing. That is why it is here, beside the wedge dome, for comparison. Every length, angle and count in this film is solved by this project's own code, at our own size, and every picture is drawn by our own software.

chapters.title: Three frequency
narration: Take the icosahedron's twenty faces and cut each into nine smaller triangles, three to an edge, then push every new point out onto the sphere. That is a three-frequency dome, and it has only three strut lengths. At our size, 16 feet across the base, A is 34.0 inches, B is 39.4 and C is 40.2. Twelve points have five neighbours and every other point has six. The triangles round the fives make pentagons; the rest make hexagons.

chapters.title: Five eighths
narration: This sphere has no level ring of points at its middle, so the usual cut goes lower, to the points nearest five-eighths of the way down. What is kept is 105 triangles: 30 in pentagons and 75 in hexagons. Its height is 0.594 of its width, a little under the five-eighths of its name. That wall below the middle is the point of the cut: it stands up nearly straight, so the floor near the edge is floor you can stand on.

chapters.title: A base that zig-zags
narration: The bottom of the cut is 15 edges, and it does not lie on one level. Its corners alternate between two heights, 40 millimetres apart, about 1.56 inches. So 10 of the base sections must be tapered, low at one end and high at the other, and 5 sit level. Build the base ring first, set it on the deck, check its diagonals, and fasten it down. Everything above it goes together easier when this first ring is right.

chapters.title: Two panels, over and over
narration: Every panel in the dome is one of two triangles. The pentagon panel has a 39.4 inch base and two 34.0 inch sides, and there are 30 of them. The hexagon panel has the same base and two 40.2 inch sides, and there are 75. These outlines are the outside faces of the panels. Nothing may stick out past them, and nothing may fall short of them.

chapters.title: Finish, then rip in half
narration: The sticks are sawn lumber. Finish the boards first, while they are whole: the face you rip will be hidden in the joint. Then tilt the table saw blade to the bevel and rip each board down its middle. A cut through the centre of a rectangle leaves two pieces that are copies of each other, turned end for end. It is the same symmetry that makes a split log give identical wedges. Turn the offcut over and send it back through for a hair more, and the two halves come out exactly alike.

chapters.title: Draw the jig with two arcs
narration: The jig is a sheet of plywood with the panel drawn on it full size. Snap a straight line for the base and mark its two ends. A thin stick with a nail at each end is a trammel. Set it to one side length and swing an arc from one end; set it to the other side and swing from the other end. Where the arcs cross is the third corner. Measure all three sides again, then join the points. For the hexagon panel the apex lands 35.1 inches above the base.

chapters.title: Rails, and the line
narration: Lay a stick along each side, flat face down and bevel out, with its outer edge splitting the line. Clamp it, butt a rail against its inside edge, and screw the rail down. Do all three sides. Now any stick pushed against a rail lands exactly on its line. The jig does not care what size the sticks are, so long as every stick is the same size and the bevel is right.

chapters.title: Sticks that turn like a pinwheel
narration: The three sticks do not meet at a point. Each runs to one corner and butts into the inside face of the next, so from above the corners turn like a pinwheel. That is why the two equal sides of a panel still take different sticks. In a hexagon panel the two C sticks are 38.47 and 38.51 inches along their outer edges, with tail cuts 31.4 and 29.3 degrees off square. Cut one end, lay the stick in, mark where the next stick crosses it, and cut that end with the miter and the bevel set together. Clamp a stop block and repeat, and check the fit every few sticks.

chapters.title: One bevel cannot be exact
narration: Here is the number that does not flatter this method. The panels do not all turn by the same angle where they meet, so the exact bevel runs from 5.7 degrees to 7.2. A shop rips every stick at one setting, 6.5 degrees, so the worst joint is 0.8 degrees off. That is too small to see and not too small to leak. Lay a bead of sealant or a gasket between the frames as they go together; that is what takes up the difference.

chapters.title: Skin it in sections
narration: Before raising, screw panels into whole pentagons and hexagons on the shop floor and cover each group with one sheet. At this cut 6 pentagons and 10 hexagons come out whole, and 15 panels are skinned one at a time. Pull the film tight across the group and staple it on the bevelled edges, where the next section hides the staples. A torn section is then one section to replace, not the whole dome.

chapters.title: A window is a panel with hinges
narration: For each window, build one extra frame. Leave the skin off that panel in the dome, cover the spare frame, and hinge it along its top edge. A small gas strut of the kind kitchen cabinets use holds it open. Weather-strip the face it closes on so rain running down the dome cannot creep under it, and tape the hinge seam once the dome is up.

chapters.title: Raise it loose, then tighten
narration: Assemble from the base up, with a helper and plenty of clamps. Put only a few screws in each joint until the last panel closes the dome: until then the shell flexes, and that flex is what lets the last panels in. Lay a bead of sealant or a gasket between frames as they meet. Then tape the open seams between sections from the bottom up, each strip lapping over the one below, so water always runs onto tape and never under it. Do not raise a loose shell in a wind.

chapters.title: A floor the shape of the base
narration: This dome stands on a radial deck that copies its base: 15 joists from the centre, one to each base corner, and a rim board along each base edge, each end cut 12 degrees off square. Under the joists, a ring of 5 girders follows the dome's own five-fold symmetry, with a post under each girder joint. Mark the centre, lay the girders out on the ground to place the posts, set the post heights to a level line, then roll in the joists.

chapters.title: Hold it down
narration: A dome is light for its size, and wind lifts. On a deck like this one, angle brackets tie every base section to the frame below. On gravel or earth, steel stakes driven at a slant and strapped to the base sections do the same job. Anchor it before the skin is finished, not after the first storm.

chapters.title: A zome without a bevel
narration: The same panel thinking frames a zome. On the bench is a one-to-5 model of a nine-sided zome, 36 panels in 4 rows of 9. Each panel is four identical sticks in a pinwheel, square through their depth, with a miter at each end and the two ends parallel. Nothing is bevelled at all: one stick and one miter for every panel in a row.

chapters.title: The gap that is allowed
narration: Square-edged panels butted on their inside edges leave a V-shaped gap on the outside. In a two-by-four on edge ours opens from 1.2 to 1.7 inches. On a small zome, screw the inside edges together and let the roof bridge the gap. On a big one, a wedge block bevelled to half the fold fills it and gives the joint more to bear on. Fasten loosely at first: the panels hinge, and the angle sets itself as the inside edges line up. The hub problem of a zome is gone.

chapters.title: What each method asks of you
narration: Side by side: the wedge dome is 19.4 feet across, with 120 members of two lengths cut from logs with a chainsaw. The panel dome is 16 feet across, with 105 panels and 315 sticks of 6 kinds, sawn from bought boards on a table saw and a miter saw, and 10 tapered base sections. The panel dome is the better-trodden road; many people have built one. The wedge dome asks for trees, and gives back fewer, bigger pieces. Choose by what you have.

chapters.title: Two good roads
narration: Every number in this film came from this project's own solver, and the same numbers are in the book. The panel dome is a road a great many builders have already walked, and it works. The wedge dome is the other road, starting from trees instead of boards. Both end in a dome. Choose by what you have.

chapters.title: Do the one thing
narration: If any of this was worth your time, send it to one person who can
carry it further than I can. That is the whole ask. One share from
somebody with reach does more for this than a month of me in a field
with a chainsaw.
